body_en: US voters rebuke Trump as Democrats win control of Congress in ‘blue wave’
President’s party stripped of control after he spent weeks pleading with Americans to pretend he was on ballot
Tell us: what do you want to know about the midterm election results?

The United States woke up to a radically altered political landscape on Wednesday after Donald Trump was dealt a devastating blow in the midterm elections, in which his Republican party was stripped of control of the Senate and the House as his handpicked “Maga” candidates were swept away by a blue tsunami.

With counting still going on in a couple of Senate races, and with 68 House seats as yet undeclared, Democrats were assured of a congressional majority far more comfortable than most pundits had predicted. They had flipped at least seven Senate seats, in such deep-red states as Texas and Kansas, which hadn’t sent a Democrat to the upper chamber for 94 years, along with more than two dozen House districts.

Having made his final pre-election appeal to voters with a bizarre speech focusing on algae and grass from Washington’s Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, Trump resurfaced on Wednesday afternoon to deliver his first remarks since the election from the construction site of his controversial White House ballroom.
What can Democrats actually do now they have won Congress?

Sidestepping the catastrophic blow to his political standing, and what it means to his party and the country’s future, the president focused instead on his self-aggrandizing building projects in the US capital. “I grew up on construction sites,” he told the crowd.

Within hours of polls closing, the political fallout began to descend on Trump and the Republican leadership. The White House put out an Instagram post saying, “PSA: TRUMP IS STILL YOUR PRESIDENT”, without adding that his power was now vastly diminished.

Vice-President JD Vance, whose old Ohio Senate seat was one of those that fell to the Democrats, began his long and no doubt fraught journey to distance himself from Trump before the 2028 presidential election. He instantly blamed the Republican rout on Trump’s war with Iran.

“The reason we lost is the war,” he said on X . “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.”

Pressed by reporters on whether he agreed with Vance’s assessment, Trump replied: “I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit, but at the same time, if I had to do it again, I’d have to do it again.”

Joining the raft of Republican senators and representatives swept away by the blue tide, one of the early casualties of the election was the House speaker, Mike Johnson, who indicated he will not seek re-election as leader of the Republican group when Democrats take over in January.

As Vance made clear in his statement, the election channelled the anger of a seething electorate, Republican voters and Democrats alike. In addition to Trump’s war, they were furious about the soaring cost of living and inflation, aggravated by the president’s tariffs and foreign exploits.

The president spent weeks before the election pleading with the American people to pretend he was on the ballot. He may now rue that tactic: the American people took him at his word, and delivered him a bloody nose of historic proportions, flinging his presidency into lame duck status.
He appeared last night to have changed his mind, declaring on social media: “I wasn’t on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!”

As the night progressed, one shock followed another as the rout extended into parts of the US once considered safe Republican strongholds. Top of the list was Texas , the state that has come to epitomise the iron fist of modern Republican rule.

In a seismic shift, James Talarico became the first Democrat to be sent by Texas to the US Senate since 1988. A Democratic dream of flipping the state that has been frustrated in countless previous cycles finally came to pass.
In a double whammy, out too went Greg Abbott, a titan of Texas Republican politics. He was ousted by Gina Hinojosa , who becomes the first Democratic governor of Texas in 36 years.

Her elevation to the state’s highest office as its first Latina governor stands in itself as a repudiation of the Trump administration . The brutal mass deportation campaign unleashed by ICE against Hispanics in Texas was one of Trump’s most resounding own goals, as it pushed away droves of voters who had backed him only two years ago.
body_zh: 随着民主党在“蓝色浪潮”中赢得国会控制权，美国选民谴责特朗普
总统的政党在花了数周时间恳求美国人假装他在投票后失去了控制权
请告诉我们：您想了解有关中期选举结果的哪些信息？
在唐纳德·特朗普(Donald Trump)在中期选举中遭受毁灭性打击后，美国周三醒来，政治格局发生了根本性的变化，他的共和党被剥夺了对参议院和众议院的控制权，他精心挑选的“MAGA”候选人被一场蓝色海啸席卷而去。
由于在几次参议院竞选中仍在进行计数，并且有68个众议院席位尚未宣布，民主党人确信国会多数席位比大多数权威人士预测的要舒适得多。他们在德克萨斯州和堪萨斯州等深红色州至少翻转了七个参议院席位，这些州已有94年没有派民主党人进入上议院，还有二十多个众议院选区。
特朗普在华盛顿林肯纪念堂反射池的藻类和草地上发表了一场奇怪的演讲，向选民发出了最后的选前呼吁，并于周三下午重新浮出水面，在他备受争议的白宫宴会厅建筑工地上发表了自选举以来的第一次言论。
民主党人现在能做些什么，他们已经赢得了国会？
总统回避了对其政治地位的灾难性打击，以及这对他的政党和国家未来的意义，而是专注于他在美国首都的自我扩张建筑项目。“我在建筑工地长大，”他告诉人群。
在民意调查结束后的几个小时内，政治影响开始降临到特朗普和共和党领导层身上。白宫在Instagram上发布了一篇帖子，称“PSA ：特朗普仍然是你的总统” ，但没有补充说他的权力现在大大削弱了。
副总统JD Vance的旧俄亥俄州参议院席位是民主党的席位之一，他在2028年总统大选之前开始了他漫长而毫无疑问的旅程，与特朗普保持距离。他立即将共和党的溃败归咎于特朗普与伊朗的战争。
“我们失败的原因是战争，”他在X上说。“如果你想争辩说，在接下来的6年里失去参议院是值得的，那就这样做吧。争辩说，这是一个值得付出的代价。同意或不同意，这至少是诚实的。”
当被记者问及他是否同意万斯的评估时，特朗普回答说： “我认为这在很大程度上是真的，因为它推动了汽油价格上涨了一点，但与此同时，如果我不得不再次这样做，我将不得不再次这样做。”
众议院议长迈克·约翰逊（ Mike Johnson ）加入了被蓝潮席卷的共和党参议员和众议员的行列，这是选举的早期伤亡之一，他表示，当民主党人在1月份接任时，他不会寻求连任共和党领袖。
正如万斯在声明中明确表示的那样，选举引发了共和党选民和民主党选民的愤怒。除了特朗普的战争，他们还对飙升的生活成本和通货膨胀感到愤怒，总统的关税和外国剥削加剧了这种情况。
总统在选举前花了几周时间恳求美国人民假装他在选票上。他现在可能会对这种策略感到后悔：美国人民听从了他的话，给了他一个历史性的血腥鼻子，把他的总统职位扔进了跛脚鸭的地位。

title_en: Where voters stand on state ballot measures, from abortion to LGBTQ rights to guns
title_zh: 选民支持州投票措施的地方，从堕胎到LGBTQ权利再到枪支
summary: Voters in dozens of states considered 146 statewide ballot measures this midterm cycle, on topics spanning LGBTQ rights, wealth taxes, abortion, redistricting, guns and more.
summary_zh: 在本中期周期，数十个州的选民就LGBTQ权利、财富税、堕胎、redis等主题审议了146项全州范围的选票措施
body_en: Where voters stand on state ballot measures, from abortion to LGBTQ rights to guns
Tuesday's midterm elections were a huge sweep for Democrats, among other takeaways .

And across 39 states — plus Washington, D.C. and the Northern Mariana Islands — voters weighed in on 146 statewide ballot measures spanning issues from taxes to transgender rights to traffic cameras to data centers and AI.
Three states moved to preserve abortion access

The U.S. Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade in 2022, leaving the legality and regulation of abortion up to each state. In subsequent elections, over a dozen states have put access to abortion on their ballots — and overwhelmingly moved to secure it.
This year, four states considered abortion measures. Three passed, while Idaho voted to preserve the state's abortion ban from 2022.

In Missouri, voters rejected a Republican-led amendment that would have banned abortion with few exceptions. The move affirms support for abortion just two years after voters mobilized to reject Missouri's ban, which was one of the strictest in the country.

Nevada residents voted to enshrine abortion up to the point of viability in their constitution. They did so for the second election in a row , since state law requires a proposed constitutional amendment to pass twice.

Virginians voted to create a "fundamental right to reproductive freedom" in their constitution. That includes the right to an abortion during the first two trimesters (and afterward in certain cases), as well as the right to contraception, fertility, postpartum care and more.
Many states considered changes to how they run their elections .
It was too early to call Wednesday afternoon whether voters had approved some of the more far-reaching changes, in Alaska and Arizona.
Other states — including Nevada, North Carolina and Ohio — passed measures toughening identification requirements for voters, while California voted against such an effort.
Several states — including Alaska, Arkansas, Kansas, South Dakota and West Virginia — approved measures reinforcing that U.S. citizenship is required to vote in their elections.

Redistricting was also top of mind for voters. President Trump kicked off a redistricting race earlier this year by urging Republican-led states to redraw their districts ahead of the midterms. Republicans and Democrats in multiple states did so. But many of the districts altered to boost GOP prospects ultimately went to Democratic candidates.
Missouri voters rejected a Republican-friendly congressional map , while Maryland voters passed a redistricting amendment that could pave the way for a Democrat-leaning map in 2028.
Virginians passed a measure automatically restoring voting rights to anyone convicted of a felony once they have completed their sentence.

Virginians also passed a constitutional amendment officially repealing its ban on gay marriage and adding language confirming that the commonwealth will recognize marriage between two adults regardless of their sex, gender or race.

Virginia's ban has been moot since the Supreme Court made same-sex marriage legal nationwide in 2015, but this measure is seen as a safeguard in case Obergefell v. Hodges gets reversed (as some have feared in the wake of the court's overturning of Roe v. Wade ). Other states have made similar moves, including Colorado and California in 2024.

Vermont overwhelmingly voted to add an amendment to its constitution guaranteeing equal protection under the law "race, ethnicity, sex, religion, disability, sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression, or national origin."

A number of states considered measures restricting transgender kids' access to school sports teams and gender-affirming care, with Colorado passing both . A Washington state measure to ban trans students from competing in girls' school sports was still leading on Wednesday.

It was a big night for doctors to win seats in Congress, riding the blue wave

Dr. Annie Andrews, who won the race for Senate in South Carolina, talked about the measles outbreak in the state in her campaign. She's pictured at an election night party in Charleston. Mic Smith/AP hide caption
The U.S. Senate will soon have a practicing physician who's a Democrat for the first time since 1938, with the election of Dr. Annie Andrews, a pediatrician, in South Carolina.

Her win — among many other physician candidates Tuesday night — marks a dramatic shift when it comes to doctors with political power across the country. Historically, doctors have been elected to Congress more often as Republicans, not Democrats. But that changed this cycle.
Check out the NPR Politics Podcast for daily analysis of the biggest news out of Washington, D.C.

In the recent past, the Republican party attracted doctor-candidates who were essentially small business people who had concerns about high taxes and government overreach. The new crop of candidates from health professions often work for large hospital systems and are interested in issues that align with Democratic priorities like public health, equity and affordability.
Andrews told NPR before she won that she was motivated to enter politics after watching parents worry about the cost of things like inhalers for asthma patients and insulin for kids with diabetes.

"I watch as worried parents leave the hospital in the evening so that they can go work their third shift job just so they can make ends meet," she said. "And then, like the majority of pediatricians in America, I've cared for kids who've been shot." Guns are the leading cause of death for children in the U.S.
6 takeaways from Democrats' big wave on election night
"It really clicked to me that the path to catalyzing this change that I want to see in America for the children in America is through politics," she explained.

In the current Senate, all four of the physicians are Republicans. Two of them, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R.-La., and Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan, lost their reelection bids this year. With the election of South Carolina's Andrews and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, an epidemiologist, in Michigan, there will now be an equal number of Republican and Democratic physicians in the upper chamber. (El-Sayed trained as a physician but did not do a residency or practice medicine, instead pursuing public health.)
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeats Republican Mike Rogers in key Michigan Senate race

In the House, the six members of the Democratic doctor's caucus will be joined by at least two more: New Jersey's Dr. Adam Hamawy, a former U.S. Army surgeon, and pediatrician Dr. Richard Pan in California. In the GOP doctor's caucus, neurosurgeon Dr. John Cowan was elected in Georgia, but at least two incumbents lost their seats, with a few races still too close to call.

Many of these new Democratic physician-lawmakers were recruited and backed by 314 Action , a name that refers to the mathematical constant pi. The organization supports progressive candidates with science backgrounds to run for office, and it invested more than $30 million in dozens of Democratic candidates competing in state and federal races, including 48 physicians.
The group's president, Shaughnessy Naughton , says that the organization does leadership development and recruits scientists to run across the country, then helps candidates in a variety of ways.

"We work to help them put together their campaign strategy, communication strategy, media training, we help to get them local and national media exposure, work with them on their fundraising, and fundraise for them," she explains.

Those candidates won big time on Tuesday. In addition to big national names like Senators-elect Andrews and El-Sayed, and Governor-elect Dr. Amy Acton of Ohio, many of the downballot candidates 314 Action supported won as well. Among them are several incoming state legislators who will be the only elected physicians in their chambers: Dr. Nikhil Wagle in Iowa, Dr. Amelia Gallitano-Mendel in Arizona, and Dr. Jarod Fox in Florida.

body_en: Trump boasts about ‘magnificent’ ballroom day after Republican rout | Donald Trump
Trump boasts about ‘magnificent’ ballroom day after Republican rout
US president rhapsodized about ballroom features for more than 20 minutes, with no mention of Democrats’ ‘blue wave’
Send us your questions about the midterm results
Less than 24 hours after suffering historic party losses in the US midterm elections , Donald Trump gathered reporters and network TV cameras at the White House to congratulate his team.
“The whole thing is a miracle, and it’s all because of you,” the US president said into a microphone on Wednesday afternoon.
He was not referring to the blue wave that swept the country as Democrats retook control of the US Congress, but his controversial White House ballroom.

Standing on the construction site on Wednesday, the US president boasted about the ballroom ’s “magnificent” columns carved out of limestone, 50ft-high ceilings, ability to hold more than 300 guests, heavy-set beams, “drone-proof” roof, thick marble floors and military-grade bunker.

He went into great detail about the construction of the ballroom, seemingly teasing the fact that it would open soon. He pivoted to discuss his love for construction projects, and his other controversial efforts to beautify Washington DC .

For more than 20 minutes, there was no mention of the elephant in the room: the fact that dozens of Trump-endorsed candidates in competitive races for the Senate and House of Representatives nationwide lost their elections to Democrats on Tuesday.
When Doug Burgum, the secretary of the interior, took the microphone, he declared Wednesday to be “a day of celebration and a day of gratitude”.
Only when the US president finally took questions from reporters did he address his party’s dismal performance in the midterms, seemingly unfazed that Democrats outperformed expectations.

“Look, I’ll get along probably with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive, but I have the power of the veto,” Trump said. He admitted it was “largely true” that the war with Iran played a role in helping Democrats, because it drove up fuel prices, but insisted the conflict was worth it.

Democrats took back the House and the Senate and won in several gubernatorial races. Senate candidates in historically red states, such as South Carolina, Texas, Kansas and North Carolina, defeated Republicans.
Even in districts gerrymandered over the last year to assist Republicans , at the behest of Trump, Democrats managed to retain control.

Trump, who spent months urging his supporters to pretend he was on the ballot, swiftly pointed out that he was not actually on the ballot as the scale of Tuesday’s Republican losses became clear. But this election was widely seen as a referendum on the president, and his agenda.

His decision to appear on Wednesday at the site of his planned ballroom mirrored an extraordinary decision to deliver his final address of the campaign at Washington’s Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool , describing – in detail – changes to its pipes, the grass surrounding the area, and granite.

For months, Trump has pulled focus to his various construction projects across the capital, including the ballroom, the refurbished Reflecting Pool, a planned triumphal arch, the cleaning of statues and monuments and a new White House helipad.
Meanwhile, Americans have grown increasingly frustrated with Trump’s performance as president – blaming his economic policies and war with Iran for increasing the cost of living.
But Trump continued to claim on Wednesday that voters were not rejecting him by voting for Democrats. “Look, if I were on the ballot we would’ve won,” Trump asserted to reporters.

Trump’s wealth dented after Democrats trounce Republicans in midterms
Trump Media stock and WLFI coin saw declines but he is still $2.7bn wealthier than when he won election in 2024
Send us your questions about the midterm results
Donald Trump ’s wealth is falling along with his political fortunes.

Tradable investment assets that helped make the president more than $2bn during his first year in office are collapsing in value the day after the Democrats trounced the Republicans in the midterm elections . Trump Media and Technology Group stock, which trades on the Nasdaq exchange, was priced at just over $5 on Wednesday morning – its lowest mark ever, and down from an all-time high of $101. It lost 11% overnight, dropping from $5.90 once the election returns started coming in. Trump has reported he owns 114m shares of DJT.

Trump owns over 40% of the stock through a trust. He has still grown his wealth dramatically during his presidency; Forbes estimated in a September analysis that he is $ 2.7bn wealthier than when he won the White House in 2024.

Another major asset for Trump and his family are World Liberty Financial digital tokens . The digital coins are trading at less than 5 cents after the election. At their height, in 2025, they were valued at six times that, at 31 cents. The WLFI coin, the governance token of World Liberty financial, began sliding in late October as the election drew near, and as a hack of Binance rattled crypto markets. It experienced a steep decline around 7pm ET on Tuesday as polls in some states closed.
US stocks rise, dollar slides as investors digest Democrats’ midterm victories
Trump already made more than $500m in profit selling crypto assets last year, according to his personal financial disclosures, though he still owns 15bn tokens.

World Liberty is a venture created by the Trump family and the family of Steven Witkoff. Trump appointed Witkoff, a personal friend and real estate developer, to negotiate diplomatic arrangements about Gaza, Iran and Ukraine.
The value of both WLIF and DJT has always been pegged to the way Trump is perceived, said Jim Angel, an associate professor at Georgetown University’s McDonough School of Business.
“People think they’re investing in Trump. They really aren’t. They’re really betting on his popularity. That’s what they’re betting on.
“Right now his popularity is at record lows,” Angel added, “and so we see the price of DJT and World Liberty at record lows.”

Separate digital novelty coins called $Trump , which made the president $636m in sales in 2025, have also collapsed in value. They are priced at about $1.40 and seem to have lost about 10% of their value overnight as election results came in. They launched shortly before his inauguration and briefly traded as high as $45 in January 2025.

2026 midterms: Schumer heralds 'generational remake' of Senate In remarks the day after his party flipped control of Congress, the Senate Minority Leader said voters had spoken clearly about their priorities, and said it's up to the Democratic party to deliver.
Chuck Schumer heralds Democrats' 'generational remake' of Senate

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., speaks during a press conference at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee in Washington, DC, on Nov. 4, 2026. Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Midterms coverage: Live results | Takeaways | Stories around the country
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told reporters Wednesday that the massive blue wave that brought Democrats control of the House and Senate signifies a "generational remake of the Senate map."

"These voters did not give us the majority so we can do whatever we want," the New York Democrat said outside the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee in Washington, D.C. "They entrusted us with the majority to do what they — the American people — want."

Democrats secured major gains in red states President Trump has previously carried, including Iowa, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. Their victories include a history-making win in Kansas, which hasn't sent a Democrat to the Senate in 94 years .
Schumer, who is poised to become Senate Majority leader in January, credited these wins to a crop of candidates who "knew how to tailor their message to the states."
Democrats now have a 54-seat majority, including the two independent senators who caucus with the party. Two races have still not been called: Alaska and Mississippi.

Schumer vowed that "relief is on the way" for voters, and acknowledged that some remain skeptical that Democrats will deliver. He said Democrats are intent on bringing down the cost of living, ending the Iran war, and undertaking investigations into the White House to address allegations of corruption.
"The days of Trump's supplicant Senate are over," Schumer declared.

President Trump hasn't shied away from saying he will use his veto pen on Democratic legislative priorities, but has also signaled some openness to cutting deals with the new Democratic-controlled Congress.
"We are going to work hard to drive costs down with the president or without him," Schumer said.

JD Vance said on Wednesday that the war against Iran doomed the Republican party in the US midterm elections , which are widely seen as a sweeping rebuke of Donald Trump’s presidency.

The intervention signals that the vice-president, once the face of the Trump administration’s deal-making efforts with Tehran, seeks to distance himself from the unpopular conflict before a possible 2028 White House run.
The midterms were a thumping rebuke of the US-Israel relationship

“The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone … The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night,” Vance said in a lengthy post on X . “If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest.

“Everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there,” added Vance, who had reportedly been sceptical about the unresolved war, which Trump launched in February alongside Israel.
Trump had made a similar statement on Tuesday to the Wall Street Journal as his party faced historic defeat in the election.
“Iran was a piece of it,” he said in the phone interview when asked about the impact of the war on the election. But he also hedged and said he had no regrets about starting the conflict.

Democrats will take control of the Senate in January, according to CBS News' projections, after major upsets in Texas , South Carolina and Kansas in the 2026 midterm elections.

The Senate races in Alaska and Mississippi remain unresolved as of Wednesday morning, with CBS News rating both as toss-ups. But Democrats have secured enough wins to control at least 54 seats in the upper chamber, a once-unthinkable feat.

Democratic candidates flipped seats in Maine , Iowa , Ohio and North Carolina . The party also held onto their seats in Georgia New Hampshire and Michigan, where Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won the contentious race against Republican Mike Rogers.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer vowed Wednesday that "whenever Trump defies the will of the American people or the law, we will launch investigations, take him to court, and entangle him in legislative razor wire."
21m ago Ted Cruz says he called to congratulate Talarico, calls results a "blue tsunami"
On his podcast, Republican Sen. Ted Cruz didn't hold back on what he thought about Tuesday night's catastrophic results for Republicans in Texas.

"History was made last night," he said. "For months, we were saying that 2026 was the most consequential midterm election of our lifetimes. Unfortunately, we were right. Sometimes, history is to be celebrated. Other times, it is to be mourned. Always, it must be reckoned with. 2026 was not simply a blue wave. It was a blue tsunami. It was an ass kicking. It was not simply a bad 2006 midterm election. It was a Watergate-level repudiation."

Cruz said they have to ask what happened and why, and where they go from here. The problem wasn't turnout, he said. "Instead, our voters, Republicans, libertarians, independents, showed up and voted, and rejected our candidates, voting Democrat instead. We've lost the House, we've lost the Senate."
"Nowhere are the consequences of this election greater than Texas," he said, adding that he'd been warning for weeks that Republicans could lose it all.
Cruz said he called Democratic Senator-elect James Talarico Tuesday night and congratulated him on his "impressive" victory.
Cruz said Republicans need to understand that the country's "K-shaped economy" is a "yawning divide."

body_en: Mississippi Senate race still a toss-up, with razor-thin margin - CBS News
Washington — The Senate midterm race in deep-red Mississippi remains unresolved, with Democrat Scott Colom mounting a surprisingly competitive challenge to incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
With about 96% of the vote in, at one point Wednesday morning just a few dozen votes separated the candidates, a stunningly close result in the Magnolia State.
Hyde-Smith, 67, has been in the Senate since 2018 and is seeking reelection. But Colom, a district attorney, launched a formidable challenge, and could deliver Democrats yet another victory.

Democrats saw a slew of wins in Senate races Tuesday night, including in states that President Trump won by double digits in the 2024 elections. With more than four flips of GOP-held seats, Democrats secured enough seats to take control of the chamber in the new year. If Colom manages to pull off a victory, he would add to their majority.

Colom, 43, is a seventh-generation Mississippian who campaigned on cost of living and health care issues. Democrats began investing in the race in recent weeks, seeing an opportunity for a pickup. But the possible outcome still appeared exceedingly unlikely heading into Election Day.
Mr. Trump won Mississippi by 20 points in 2024, and the state hasn't elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1982.
Speaking to supporters in the wee hours of the morning on Wednesday, Colom said, "The results are all trending in our direction."
"We are trending in counties that people thought we had no chance to compete in," Colom said. "And we're winning them."
The unresolved race in Mississippi comes as Alaska's Senate race is also outstanding, leaving the size of Democrats' majority up in the air.

Well, it was a Democratic tsunami at the ballot box. Voters have delivered a sweeping rebuke of President Trump and his party in the 2026 midterms, handing Democrats major victories across the country and dramatically reshaping the balance of power in Washington.
Mr. Trump now enters a lame-duck phase of his second term, promising both to use his veto power and also to work across the aisle as he faces the largest Democratic majorities in decades.
After two years of unified Republican government...
... a sea change is coming to Washington, a blue wave that grew into a tidal wave, Democrats poised to seize control of both houses of Congress by wide margins.
The American people reduced the red brick wall to a pile of bricks.
... the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption and incompetence of the failed lame-duck President Donald J. Trump.

He added that the Republican Party has to have an honest conversation about that thorny topic after it led to higher prices and drove voters to want change.
I can tell you that, as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different.

If I put the kitchen on top, you would lose three walls.
But he also acknowledged the issue that cost him at the polls.
Probably, that's the primary reason, the price, not the war, the price.

To call it a wave, I don't think would be fully accurate. It's the political equivalent of a meteor strike that went all around the United States. This is close to an extinction-level event for Republicans in many parts of the country as we have seen probably in the last hundred years.

title_en: OpenAI is already trying to shape the 2028 election
title_zh: OpenAI已经在努力塑造2028年的选举
summary: OpenAI’s Chris Lehane wants AI to define the 2028 election, proposing a new social contract that could benefit Americans while also advancing the AI giant’s own business interests.
summary_zh: OpenAI的Chris Lehane希望人工智能能够定义2028年的选举，提出一项新的社会契约，既能让美国人受益，同时也能推进人工智能的发展。
body_en: OpenAI’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane thinks the 2028 presidential election could be a defining moment for AI. And he wants politicians to start developing policies that address Americans’ concerns about the technology, rather than simply paying lip service to anti-AI sentiment and the backlash against data centers .

In a new essay , Lehane compares AI’s potential to reshape the economy to President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal, the 1930s set of federal programs and reforms enacted after industrialization and the Great Depression shattered the old economic order. He observes that Americans today feel similarly anxious about losing control over their economic futures and urges politicians to find a “compelling third path” that allows people to share in AI’s benefits. He lays out five policy priorities, spanning worker protections and education to AI safety and data center development.

The essay comes on the heels of a stunning Democratic victory in the midterm elections, in which Democrats flipped control of Congress amid widespread voter frustration over the cost of living. Kate Brennan, who leads AI and corporate power policy at the AI Now Institute, told TechCrunch that Lehane’s rhetoric marks a notable shift from OpenAI’s policy agenda last year, which focused on accelerating AI development, reducing regulatory barriers, and expanding infrastructure.

Unsurprisingly, many of Lehane’s proposals would encourage wider AI adoption and support the infrastructure expansion companies like OpenAI need to grow. The original New Deal established protections for workers and placed constraints on corporate power. It’s less clear how Lehane’s vision would hold AI companies accountable for the economic disruption their technology could create.

“Invoking a New Deal metaphor is to invoke state capacity to actually benefit the public,” Brennan said. “This is written by a private company that is trying to advocate for policies for its own benefit. It is ahistorical at best and harmful at worst.”

While AI wasn’t a dominant issue in the midterms, opposition to data centers emerged as a major bipartisan concern in several races in the midterms. And Lehane may be right that AI will become a bigger part of the conversation over the next two years.

Affordability is already shaping up as a key issue for the 2028 election as Americans grapple with inflation, tariffs, and the rising cost of living. AI could become an increasingly large part of that conversation as voters stress about data centers hiking up electricity bills, AI replacing their jobs, and technology’s economic gains flowing only to a handful of wealthy companies.

Lehane acknowledges many of these concerns, but he offers few concrete proposals to prevent AI’s gains from becoming concentrated. Instead, he largely pitches AI as a path to greater prosperity for Americans willing to embrace it.

Take his proposals for the tax code. He suggests incentives for workers to learn AI skills, easier capital access for entrepreneurs, and new approaches to employee ownership and profit-sharing. Those are not the same as binding requirements that would ensure workers share in AI-generated wealth or that companies pay the costs of displacing workers.

“I was struck by how much of this policy is for a future…that is already predicated on mass AI adoption and AI benefiting society, which we have yet to see,” Brennan said. “All of it is predicated on benefiting from AI’s upside.”

Brennan said it would make more sense to see things like a revised corporate tax rate or tax incentives for hiring human beings rather than automating jobs, as well as ways to keep companies from amassing outsize market power.

Lehane’s emphasis on expanding AI’s economic opportunities, rather than limiting potential harms, extends to data centers. He notes concerns about data centers while emphasizing the construction jobs and local tax revenue they could generate. He then warns that politicians who support a data center moratorium could jeopardize America’s lead over China, going so far as to compare that stance to the 2002 vote to authorize the Iraq war.

Lehane also makes child safety and education central to his proposed agenda, stressing the importance of age-appropriate protections and safeguards around AI companions for minors. He also warns against keeping AI out of classrooms , arguing that doing so could lead to inequality between wealthy students and “children in rural communities.” But the argument takes for granted that AI improves learning, a claim that remains unproven and one critics say deserves more examination than more funding or individualized attention from human teachers.

Lehane also calls for enforceable AI safety standards, independent evaluations, public oversight, and the ability to restrict AI systems or use a kill switch to shut them down — though recent studies show that OpenAI and other AI labs haven’t published comprehensive plans for what they would do if a model escaped human control.

Brennan called these stances “disingenuous,” pointing to OpenAI’s history of opposing legislation designed to impose such measures. In 2024, for example, OpenAI opposed California’s AI safety bill, SB 1047, which would have mandated catastrophic risk evaluations and shutdown capabilities. Last year, OpenAI also sought to limit state regulation , arguing that states could undermine American innovation. The company has more recently shifted some of those positions, backing several state safety laws and saying it would be open to independent evaluators embedded in the company.

Lehane also argues that people should maintain control over consequential decisions made using AI, rather than handing off judgment entirely to machines. But that raises the question of what human control really looks like in a society where humans are increasingly being required to use AI in education, work, healthcare, and government.

Throughout his essay, Lehane frames AI as a technology that could give Americans back their sense of agency and economic opportunity. But he ties average Americans’ “middle class” success to participation in an economy increasingly shaped by companies like OpenAI. Whether his policies will meaningfully redistribute power or subtly entrench it is less clear.
TechCrunch reached out to OpenAI for more specifics on Lehane’s proposals and the company’s stances, but it did not respond by the time of publication.

title_en: Elon Musk will face scrutiny from Democrats after midterms
title_zh: 埃隆·马斯克（ Elon Musk ）将在中期选举后面临民主党人的审查
summary: Democrats are likely to launch investigations into Musk's influence, including his leadership of DOGE and government contracts
summary_zh: 民主党人可能会对马斯克的影响力展开调查，包括他对总督和政府合同的领导
body_en: Elon Musk will face scrutiny from Democrats after midterms

Elon Musk gave more than $445 million to Republican candidates, political action committees and outside groups, according to federal election filings but most of the candidates he backed on Tuesday lost. Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images hide caption

Elon Musk wasn't on Tuesday's ballot, but he stands to lose a lot from Democrats' sweeping midterm victories in the House and Senate. In no state was this more acutely felt than in Texas, home to the headquarters of Musk's companies and where he spent more than $200 million, according to federal filings, in a mission to sway the Senate race in the Republican candidate's favor.

With a Democratic majority in Congress, the billionaire, who controls Tesla and SpaceX, will likely face investigations into the billions of dollars of government contracts his companies have been awarded since President Trump returned to office and his role leading the Department of Government Efficiency at the beginning of Trump's second term.

Musk gave more than $445 million to Republican candidates, political action committees and outside groups, according to federal election filings analyzed by OpenSecrets , a nonprofit that tracks campaign spending. That makes him the top donor in the midterms and among the very largest political donors in American history.

The central question Democratic lawmakers say they want answered is whether Musk used his influence inside the Trump administration to benefit his own businesses, and whether taxpayer money, government data and public institutions were put at risk in the process.

During the four months Musk led DOGE, he received at least $6.3 billion in government contracts. Since then, he has gained at least another $10 billion in government contracts, according to the Democracy Defenders Fund , a legal advocacy nonprofit.

"The DOGE chickens are coming home to roost. Elon Musk waved a chainsaw on stage and laughed while firing public servants and gutting the services Americans rely on. Then he lied to the American people about the savings. He must answer for it under oath," Rep. James Walkinshaw (D-Va.) wrote on X .

Musk's foreign dealings are also under scrutiny. Democratic Sen. Chris Coons of Delaware posted on X that Musk's links to Russia's President Vladimir Putin are "One more thing to add to the list of questions for Musk when I subpoena him."

U.S. Rep. Mike Levin of California highlighted that Musk restricted Ukraine's use of his Starlink satellite internet service days after Trump eased sanctions on Russia and began buying Russian diesel in October. Starlink and its military-grade counterpart, Starshield, are vital for Ukraine's civilian infrastructure, frontline communications and drone operations in its war against Russia.

"How on earth did we get to this point? How is it possible that Musk can disrupt an American ally's military operations whenever he chooses, maintain a clear line to the Kremlin, and face zero accountability to the American people or the U.S. government?" Levin wrote on X .
Musk did not respond to a request for comment from NPR.

While leading DOGE, Musk was a part-time special government employee, and as such was subject to a federal law prohibiting covered executive branch and related personnel from participating in official matters affecting their personal financial interests, said Richard Painter, former chief White House ethics lawyer in the George W. Bush administration.

"SpaceX is a big contractor and gets a lot of money from NASA and the Department of Defense. If [Musk] touched anything that he knew would have an impact on SpaceX, he would've committed a crime," Painter said.
Texas has played a growing role in Musk's business empire

Texas in particular has become a big focus of Musk's efforts to exert political power, as he has made the state the nerve center of his sprawling business empire. Tesla's corporate headquarters and a major vehicle manufacturing facility are in Austin. X, formerly Twitter, is based outside of Austin. SpaceX, which makes rockets and satellites, is based in southern Texas. Musk's Neuralink and The Boring Company are also headquartered in the state.
Much of Musk's estimated wealth is tied up in his ownership stakes in his companies. Even as markets rose Wednesday after Democrats' midterm wins, SpaceX shares fell nearly 4% and Tesla dropped 3%.

SpaceX is reportedly exploring several possible Texas sites for large data centers. Tesla owns and operates its massive Giga Texas data center in Austin. In August, plans for a $16.8 billion SpaceXAI semiconductor fabrication project in Texas were announced .

Musk directed at least $225 million of his midterm spending to Texas, according to OpenSecrets, including supporting Republican Ken Paxton's bid for U.S. Senate and Gov. Greg Abbott's reelection campaign.
But Paxton and Abbott both lost, suggesting Musk's money wasn't enough to overcome a wave of enthusiasm that saw Democrats capture every statewide office in Texas.

body_en: Republicans barely had time to absorb their sweeping midterm losses before President Trump returned to a familiar comfort zone: D.C. construction projects.

Why it matters: Voters just delivered an overwhelming rebuke of the administration, demanding that politicians focus on the cost of living, yet the president remains fixed on remaking the nation's capital in his image.

Driving the news: Trump hosted reporters at the White House on Wednesday for a previously unscheduled event to update them on the East Wing ballroom's construction, marking his first remarks to the White House press pool since the election.

He spent the majority of his remarks discussing planned architectural changes around D.C., including a proposed Triumphal Arch, the National Garden of American Heroes and a planned expansion of a publicly owned golf course that would likely eliminate popular running and biking paths.

His remarks came after a pre-election appearance Monday, during which he praised the new pipes installed at the Reflecting Pool and a proposed promenade from the Lincoln Memorial to the Potomac River.

What they're saying: Trump addressed criticism he sometimes receives for working on his construction projects, saying he was "doing it because the White House is the ultimate symbol of America, and it's got to be pristine."
"It's got to be perfect. And if you take a look at it, that's what it is right now. You have no idea how much work we had to do."
He also noted that he spends "very little time" working on the White House, but said he does it because "it's relaxing …I love construction."
Catch up quick: Democrats outperformed expectations in Tuesday's midterms, flipping the Senate before the night was over and then the House a few hours later, according to the AP.
Democrats have gained complete control of at least five previously divided state governments while ending Republican trifectas in several other states.
In ruby-red Texas, the white whale of potential pickups, Democrats flipped the governor's mansion, a Senate seat and now control the state House.

Zoom in: "President Trump's commitment to restoring our Nation's treasured landmarks should be celebrated and does not distract from his work to lower costs, strengthen our economy, and improve the lives of American families," a White House spokesperson told Axios in an emailed statement.

"While making our Nation's capital safe and beautiful again as he promised to do, President Trump remains focused on lowering costs, driving down inflation, creating good-paying jobs, reshoring our manufacturing industry, unleashing American energy dominance, securing new investment, securing our borders, deporting dangerous illegal criminals from our communities, and enforcing tough-on-crime policies."
Zoom out: Trump also briefly discussed his immigration policies and efforts to lower crime around D.C. during his Wednesday speech.
He later took questions from reporters, during which he reiterated that Republicans would have won had he been on the ballot.

title_en: Democratic leaders reflect on midterm results and what's next for the party
title_zh: Democratic leaders reflect on midterm results and what's next for the party
summary: Democratic party leaders and political analysts spoke with Morning Edition about the results of the midterm elections, the effects of mid-decade redistricting efforts, and the next steps for the party.
summary_zh: Democratic party leaders and political analysts spoke with Morning Edition about the results of the midterm elections, the effects of mid-decade redistricting efforts, and the next steps for the party.
body_en: Democratic leaders share election result reactions and takeaways : NPR

Democratic leaders share election result reactions and takeaways Democratic party leaders and political analysts spoke with Morning Edition about the results of the midterm elections, the effects of mid-decade redistricting efforts, and the next steps for the party.
Democratic leaders reflect on midterm results and what's next for the party

Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks during a midterm election night watch party at the Department at Hudson's on November 4 in Detroit, Michigan. Salwan Georges/Getty Images/Getty Images North America hide caption

Democrats coasted into victory late last night, taking control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate by considerable margins. Several states that are traditionally characterized as "deep red," including Texas, Kansas and Iowa, flipped towards Democrats in the Senate for the first time in decades. Democratic candidates also took a convincing majority in House races, despite competing in several states whose districts were redrawn to favor Republicans.

Across the country, Democratic gubernatorial candidates also burst ahead, winning races in GOP strongholds like Georgia, Ohio and Texas. Heading into 2027, Democrats will officially retake control of Congress and hold at least 28 governorships.

Newly elected Democratic officials, party leaders and pollsters joined Morning Edition on Wednesday morning to share their insights on the massive wave of Democratic victories in state and local races. In their interviews with NPR's Steve Inskeep and Michel Martin, these Democrats discussed takeaways from the midterm results, the effects of mid-decade redistricting efforts, the mandate received from voters and the next steps for the party. You can read some key takeaways from the discussions below.

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed made history in Michigan, becoming the first Muslim elected to the Senate as Democrats retake control of Congress. He said his opponent, Republican Mike Rogers, campaigned weaponizing El-Sayed's name and faith rather than addressing issues Americans really care about, like Medicare for All and the price of everyday items.
El-Sayed also discussed his opinions on legislation surrounding the war in Iran, and he agreed with Trump's scheduled end to roughly $4 billion in annual military aid to Israel.
Martin asked him about his lack of support from some Jewish and Black voters, something El Sayed said he hopes to remedy.
"There's always more work to do. There's always more to build. There's always more conversations to have," he said.

Eric Holder, chairman of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee and attorney general under former President Obama, discussed how mid-decade redistricting affected the results of the midterm. Speaking with Martin, he said that GOP gerrymandering efforts backfired, causing candidates to lose in districts that were specifically drawn for their success.
"The redistricting efforts that [Republicans] had didn't just fail — they were dismantled," Holder says.

Democrats in Georgia won seats up and down the ballot, and Stacey Abrams, founder of Fair Fight Action, said the party has been building towards this outcome since 2010. In her interview with Martin, she added that she's proud of Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first Black woman elected governor in United States history. Abrams campaigned for the same gubernatorial spot in 2018 and again in 2020, though she was never elected to the position.

Abrams said Democratic victories for the governor, attorney general, secretary of state and in the state house "gives us an opportunity to start correcting and restoring rights that we've seen lost across the South for more than 20 years."

Ken Martin, chairman of the Democratic National Committee, said yesterday's election marks the biggest win for his party in more than a century. Voters gave Democrats a mandate to address affordability, health care and the systems that exclusively benefit wealthy Americans, he explained to Martin and Inskeep, and he thinks newly elected Democrats can deliver.
"Our candidates across the board ran for something, not against something," he said. "They gave people a sense of a positive vision of what Democrats would do while we're in power."

Pollster and Democratic strategist Margie Omero explained why last night's results are a direct reflection of voter's distrust of leaders in Washington. She said contested races consistently broke towards Democrats, despite high GOP spending during campaign season.
"Voters really wanted to send a real clear message, and they couldn't have been any clearer than what we heard last night," Omero said.

Community college professor unseats incumbent Republican David Valadao in seat redrawn under Prop 50
Send us your questions about the midterm results

Democrat Randy Villegas, a community college professor with notable progressive endorsements, has won the race for California ’s 22nd congressional district in an contest that shaped up to be one of the toughest political battles in the state.

He unseated the six-term, incumbent Republican congressman, David Valadao, in a district that was considered the only true toss-up across the state of California after being redrawn under Proposition 50 , a voter-approved ballot initiative that remade the state’s voting maps last year.
‘The valley has been left behind’: how one of California’s poorest areas became its toughest political battleground
Villegas called it a victory for “hundreds of volunteers, tens of thousands of grassroots donors, and working families who believed we could build something better together”.

“With today’s election results, the Central Valley proved what’s possible when working people come together and refuse to let billionaires, Washington, and special interests decide our future,” Villegas said in a statement on Tuesday night. “The people of the Valley made their voices heard loud and clear: the Central Valley is not for sale.”
The Associated Press called the race of Villegas on Wednesday morning.

Valadao and Villegas are both Central valley natives from immigrant families with working class or agricultural ties, roots that reflect many of the constituents in California’s 22nd district, a majority-Latino district that stretches from Bakersfield to just west of Fresno.

But similarities between the two seemingly end there. They took starkly different approaches to winning in what is one of the country’s poorest congressional districts, and was, this year, home to the state’s most competitive election.

Residents said healthcare and rising costs were top of mind. The district has the second-highest rate and number of Medicaid enrollees of any congressional district, per KFF . The impact constituents are feeling from cuts to the federal health insurance program, passed last year via the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, was one of Villegas’s main talking points against Valadao, who cast one of the bill’s decisive votes.
Xavier Becerra wins California race for governor with vows to resist Trump’s agenda

Corporate financing was another big factor in this election. Valadao ended with $1.7m in cash on hand, per federal finance reports . OpenSecrets reported he has received over twice as much money from Pacs than the average House candidate.

Villegas, on the other hand, vowed not to take corporate campaign donations, running a platform that repeatedly emphasized the power of the working class. That earned him the endorsement of leading progressive figures including Bernie Sanders, Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Dolores Huerta.

His victory comes amid a historic night of wins for Democrats across the US, including in longtime Republican strongholds. Democrats took control of both the House and Senate as a larger than expected blue wave resulted in significant losses for Donald Trump and his party. Democrats also flipped several congressional seats in California with help from Proposition 50.
In a statement after the race was officially called, Villegas said: “They say it takes a village, we know it takes a Valley.”

Navajo voters hop tractors, make extraordinary efforts to vote after widespread flooding
Lilien Begay, 92, seated at left with daughters (clockwise) Berneice, Darlene, and Vera at the voting site in Denehotso, Arizona on Nov. 3, 2026 Adam Burke/KSUT hide caption
People on the Navajo Reservation had to make extra effort to vote this year.
It's a region of the southwest that's been hit this fall by repeated flooding . Roads washed out, driving thousands of people from their homes.
But voters turned out, in the parts of Arizona, Utah and New Mexico that the reservation stretches across. Yesterday at the Dennehotso Chapterhouse, voters rolled up in trucks with mud-caked tires.
The town is framed by the picturesque sandstone cursive of Comb Ridge, the stone spires of Monument Valley peeking over the ridgeline.
In the parking lot, people gathered to eat fry bread and mutton stew, something common at Navajo polling sites.
"I love to see our people come out and talk amongst each other," said 27-year-old Urbina Yazzie, adding that this year's election is unusual.
"People are having to drive on tractors to get from one road to another, just to come and vote," she said.
Dennehotso has been knocked around by floods this fall, three in the last month. But the big one that residents will talk about for decades to come, started on October 22.
Local contractor Kev Woolboy was helping coordinate response efforts, checking watersheds along the highway, as floodwaters from as far as 60 miles away raced toward town.
"We have some man-made earth dams that were supposed to slow (the water) down," Woolboy said. "But there was so much rain, those earth dams didn't stand a chance."
The floodwaters ravaged homes and newly-built roads, knocking out power and water, and leaving part of the town covered in thick, goopy mud.
"We thought we were safe," said 74-year-old Phyllis Yazzie.
Yazzie was at home with her son that day, having a late breakfast, when her niece called.

"And she says, 'Auntie! You better get out of there!'" Yazzie recalled. "I said, 'Why?' And she says, 'the flood's heading that way.' And so I went outside, I started looking towards the wash, and I saw the water rising.'"
They tried to drive out their dirt road, but were forced back to the highest point on their land, while a torrent of water carved ravines on both sides of their house.

title_zh: What the downfall of near three-decade senator Susan Collins says about Republican unpopularity

body_en: What the downfall of near three-decade senator Susan Collins says about Republican unpopularity
Troy Jackson, in just 101 days, bested the Republican, preventing her sixth Senate term: ‘You can’t eat road salt’
Send us your questions about the US midterms results and Democrats’ ‘blue wave’

T he political demise of Susan Collins – a fixture of Maine and Washington politics for three decades – recalls the famous line in Ernest Hemingway’s The Sun Also Rises about how one of the novel’s characters experienced bankruptcy: gradually, then suddenly.

In the run-up to Tuesday’s stunning Democrat “blue wave” election triumph, it seemed obvious that Collins’s 30-year tenure as Maine’s Republican senator was vulnerable to the challenge of Troy Jackson, the Democrats’ explicitly working-class candidate as voters prepared to unleash pent-up anger with Donald Trump ’s presidency.
Rather like the Berlin Wall in the days before it finally fell in 1989, however, no one seemed to believe it could really happen until it did.

Collins, after all, had survived seemingly credible electoral challenges before and appeared primed – despite opinion polls showing a close race – to win a sixth Senate term, having once pledged to serve only two. She had become something of a state institution, with her assertions that Washington connections brought federal funds and contracts to Maine carrying weight with many constituents.

Jackson, meanwhile, seemed a less-than-polished prospect for a state that had previously sent such august figures as Ed Muskie, George Mitchell and Bill Cohen to the US Senate before they went on to become international statesmen.

Jackson’s candidacy had been founded on the withdrawal of the party’s original nominee, Graham Platner, whose progressive populist platform generated real excitement before the emergence of serious sexual misconduct allegations.
Platner denied the allegations, but withdrew from the race. Jackson, a former logger, meanwhile had just 101 days to campaign after being nominated as his replacement.

On the eve of polling day, one activist, Doug Emerson, was so skeptical of local voters’ willingness to jettison Collins that he festooned his car with Trump policy miscues he believed she had been complicit in, and parked it outside the senator’s office in Portland – Maine’s biggest city – in the hope that it would raise awareness.

Even as polls closed and the count got under way, hopes for Jackson’s success seemed restrained at the Democrats’ watch party. Early returns showed Jackson with a small lead, but within catching distance, even as previous Republican electoral bastions once thought impregnable fell to the gathering Democratic wave.

The realization that this elemental political force was about to sweep away Collins came late in the evening, when – with about 60% of the ballots counted – returns showed Jackson with a convincing lead. Within minutes, MS Now reported that Collins had called to concede; wild cheers and chants of “Troy, Troy” filled the ballroom at Portland’s Holiday Inn.

Amid the euphoria, it was left to Jackson to deliver a message of humble, down-to-earth populism that emphasized his trade union background and underlined that his unlikely triumph had been driven by grassroots discontent.

“You understood what it would mean to send one of your own to the United States Senate,” he told the crowd. “Donald Trump and the billionaires need to understand one thing very clear – something about your new senator. I don’t owe them a damn thing.

“When they threaten your healthcare, your livelihood or your freedoms, I am going to stand up to them. You know where I’ll stand. You know how I’ll vote. And when you’ve got a question about it, you’ll be able to ask me yourself. I’m not acting like I’m the best thing that ever happened to the US Senate or anything like that.”

It was a promise of accessibility that critics say Collins never provided – despite her claims of independent-mindedness and protestations of frequently voting against Trump, who failed to carry Maine in any of his three presidential campaigns.

Jackson, who as a state legislator once opposed abortion rights, won the backing of pro-choice campaigners by stressing Collins’s 2018 vote for the conservative US supreme court justice, Brett Kavanaugh, who subsequently voted for the court’s ruling that overturned the historic Roe v Wade decision, which had previously guaranteed abortion rights nationally. Jackson placards reading “abortion is on the ballot” were widespread.

Trump, in contrast to his on-the-ground support giving stump speeches for multiple other Republican Senate candidates, did not visit Maine to campaign for Collins. Yet there was clear skepticism about her self-anointed image as a free-thinking critic of the US president. His shadow still loomed large.

Todd Cox, 63, a technology professional, who had previously voted for Collins, said “concern for the direction the country is going in” drove him to back Jackson this week. “We definitely haven’t become kinder and gentler under this administration,” Cox told the Guardian on Tuesday. “There’s a lot of bullying that goes on. It goes back to affordability. It’s the war in Iran – that shouldn’t be happening. It’s the disregard for the rule of law. It just seems like they’re thumbing their nose at it.”

title_zh: ‘This is an earthquake’: Latino voters rush back to Democrats
summary: The Latino inroads Trump made over the last decade have been completely reversed
summary_zh: The Latino inroads Trump made over the last decade have been completely reversed
body_en: AUSTIN — Texas. Florida. Pennsylvania. Colorado. Arizona. Nevada. California.
The historic landslide of Latino voters toward Democrats hit battleground after battleground Tuesday, crumbling the coalition that helped carry President Donald Trump to victory just one cycle ago.

“This is an earthquake,” Democratic Latino operative Sergio Gonzalez told POLITICO on the sidelines of Texas Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa’s victory party in Austin. “Latinos were angry. They were angry this election.”

While the entire country shifted toward Democrats, nowhere shifted as dramatically as predominantly Latino areas. Across the nation Latino voters of all backgrounds — Mexican Americans and Central Americans in the Southwest, heartland and on the West Coast, Puerto Ricans and Dominicans in Pennsylvania, Venezuelans, Puerto Ricans and Cubans in Florida — unhappy with the economy and furious over Trump’s immigration enforcement fled the party in droves.
In a single cycle, Democrats appeared to reset Republicans’ gradual decade-long gains with Latino voters.

Latino voters who “broke for President Trump in historical numbers [in 2024] … had to make a hard change because their paycheck wasn't moving fast and far enough for them,” said Trump’s former Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer in an interview Tuesday night. “And Republicans ran out of runway on that.”

The epicenter of the earthquake was Texas, where a turnout surge — especially among younger first-time Latino voters — helped Democrats sweep Texas’ statewide offices — the first time since 1994 they’ve won any at all. Republicans won only one of the five House seats they had gerrymandered.

“What we're seeing today is a political realignment,” said Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar, who romped to a 30-point victory Tuesday night in a newly redrawn district Trump carried by double digits two years ago.
“Republicans were renting the Hispanic vote — yet governed like they owned it,” said Giancarlo Sopo, the GOP strategist behind Trump’s viral 2020 Spanish-language campaign jingle .

But Democrats have been here before. Then President Barack Obama and his Democratic nominee Hillary Clinton posted similarly strong numbers with Latinos, before Trump’s blue-collar populism helped break through for the GOP.
Some Democrats warn that their party should not misread this week’s results to assume that Latinos are once again loyal Democratic voters.

“Tonight ought to scare the hell out of both political parties,” said Javier Palomarez, president and CEO of the U.S. Hispanic Business Council, on Tuesday. “Americans are running out of patience, and the politicians who keep mistaking their votes for unconditional loyalty are going to find themselves unemployed."

Latinos’ swing right two years ago had been fueled by frustration over inflation combined with some voters’ dissatisfaction with the Biden administration’s border policy. A cycle earlier, in 2020, Trump made significant inroads in Florida and Texas as well. But growing economic woes under Trump, combined with his hardline interior immigration enforcement, swung those communities hard this time around.

“In the Hispanic community, the hyper-aggressive ICE raids, I think, will go down as one of the darkest blemishes in modern history,” Democratic Rep. Vicente Gonzalez, who cruised to reelection Tuesday in a seat Trump had won by 10 points, told POLITICO Tuesday night. “The American people are struggling right now, and and and they delivered a very heavy punishment at the ballot box today.”

Heavily Latino counties swung more toward Democrats than any other type of place, according to preliminary returns. A handful of counties in Texas that are more than 90 percent Latino swung more than 25 points toward Democrats from 2024, the results show. Latino-majority Miami-Dade County in South Florida swung nearly 20 points.If current results hold, roughly half of the 10 Latino Republicans who served in the last Congress won’t be returning, while Democrats’ Latino caucus will grow significantly.

“We put in the hard work. Talk to Latino voters early and often, and they're showing up,” Rep. Linda Sanchez (D-Calif.), who chairs the Congressional Hispanic Caucus’ BOLD PAC, told POLITICO. “They trust Democrats more on the economy now. They see us as real champions and fighters.”

Trump won Starr County, Texas — part of Cuellar’s district — with 58 percent of the vote two years ago, the first time in more than a century that a Republican had won a presidential election there. On Tuesday, Democrat James Talarico won 77 percent there.

That county, like many others in the Rio Grande Valley, had long favored Democrats but moved toward the GOP during the Trump era. That’s now all been erased, as Brownsville native Gina Hinojosa will become the first Hispanic governor of Texas since it became a U.S. state. “We've called the RGV a bellwether for so long,” Melissa Morales, the executive director of SOMOS PAC, told POLITICO. “But to actually get the first Latina governor of Texas from the RGV I think is a bellwether in its own of what the next generation of leadership looks like.”

In California’s 22nd District, a Central Valley district which is roughly three-quarters Latino, progressive Democrat Randy Villegas was leading incumbent GOP Rep. David Valadao 66%-34% with roughly two-thirds of the vote in. A handful of rural majority-Latino counties in Kansas — Seward, Finney and Ford — that Trump had won by more than 30 points in 2024 were narrowly won by Democratic Senate candidate Adam Hamilton. The counties were among those shaken by ICE raids earlier in the fall.
“Recent ICE activity in southwest Kansas turned around the electorate out here,” said Republican state Sen. Bill Clifford, who represents Finney County.

title_en: The midterms were a thumping rebuke of the US-Israel relationship
title_zh: The midterms were a thumping rebuke of the US-Israel relationship

Even Trump seems to recognize that the relationship has become a political liability, and may never be the same
Send us your questions about the midterm results

On the eve of a midterm election that ended in an unequivocal rejection of his brand of politics, even Donald Trump seemed to recognize that the US-Israel relationship had become a political liability.

Trump’s 11th-hour suggestion, on election morning, that he would cut military aid to Israel at the end of the year because, as he put it, “they don’t need it”, was condemned across the board – with pro-Palestinian advocates dismissing it as “desperate” and pro-Israel ones as “unserious”.

Trump’s suggestion that he would replace nearly $4bn in annual military aid with arms sales signaled little would change in practice – the funding would continue and it would be harder to track. But it was still a notable recognition by the president of just how much support for Israel has tanked against the backdrop of the latest war in Gaza, which has killed more than 70,000 Palestinians, been widely been described as a genocide, and reshaped US politics in ways unthinkable just three years ago.

Indeed, come January, the US House will include an army doctor who went on a medical mission in Gaza , a lawyer who was fired by her firm over a blogpost criticizing Israel’s war, a Jewish lawmaker who was recently detained by Israeli forces while helping Palestinians harvest olives in the occupied West Bank, and a community organizer who participated in a pro-Palestine student encampment and scored one of the primary season’s most stunning upsets under the banner “babies, not bombs”.

Pro-Palestinian candidates – including Palestinian-American ones – have won downballot races. And in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim to be elected to the US Senate, following a campaign that saw more than $40m spent by Aipac in an effort to defeat him, last-minute drama , and unprecedented levels of Islamophobic rhetoric and bigotry.

“The old bipartisan consensus on Israel is over,” Beth Miller, political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action, said. Without that consensus in place, the next Congress could push a number of measures, from an arms embargo on Israel to sanctions against violent settlers and officials – though Trump would retain veto power to block them.

The vote was also a rejection of Trump’s war in Iran – something even JD Vance said on Wednesday was “ obvious to almost everyone ”. Foreign policy issues rarely determine US elections – that is, until those issues have a direct effect on Americans’ lives at home.

“Americans were reminded of the failures of the Iran war with every visit to the gas station and grocery store,” said Yousef Munayyer, head of the Palestine/Israel Program at the Arab Center Washington DC. “Israel is a central piece of that story.”

Across the country, and up and down the ballot, unabashedly pro-Palestinian candidates defeated pro-Israel ones despite groups like Aipac pouring tens of millions of dollars into a failed attempt to reverse Israel’s collapsing standing among US voters. Last month, Aipac acknowledged its open support was hurting pro-Israel candidates more than it helped them, and announced it would stop making direct endorsements and contributions – a remarkable admission even if one with little practical consequence.

The victories of El-Sayed and several other candidates whom the right sought to cast as antisemitic over their support for Palestinians also marked a significant rejection of the narrative that pro-Israel voices and the Trump administration have relentlessly advanced over the last three years – that criticism of Israel is, by default, antisemitic.

“They try to call you hateful if you believe that Palestinian kids should get to grow up in the land of their forefathers without being murdered by our tax dollars,” El-Sayed, who has continued to speak plainly about his support for Palestinians despite coming under enormous pressure over it, said during his acceptance speech. “If you believe in equal rights to peace, dignity, and self determination, that’s not hate, it’s love.”

In Michigan, El-Sayed won a majority of Jewish voters , according to exit polls. Despite warnings that Jews would leave the Democratic party en masse over its shifts on Israel, J Street said its polling found that 72% of Jews voted for Democrats on Tuesday, even though the Republican party increased its share of the Jewish vote since 2024..
This does not mean that the Democratic party is unified on Israel and Palestine and or in opposition to foreign wars.

For decades, the party has “excluded or marginalized anyone whose progressive values extend to support for Palestine”, Lara Friedman, the president of the Foundation for Middle East Peace, said. “American voters, organizers, and a cohort of enormously talented candidates came together and kicked the door down.”
Democrats have become the party of war. Americans are tired of it

Matt Duss, executive vice-president of the Center for International Policy and a former foreign policy aide to Senator Bernie Sanders, said that the Democrats now must seize the opportunity to become the party opposed to war.

“Trump ran and won as an anti-war candidate in 2024, because unfortunately Democrats left that lane wide open for him,” he said. “The question is: will Democrats finally get it? Will they finally realize that Americans are tired of war and want a new foreign policy?”

Miami helicopter crash leaves one person dead and two injured
Helicopter was carrying three people and crashed in waters of Biscayne Bay, east of Miami executive airport
A helicopter crash in Miami on Wednesday morning has left one person dead and two others injured.

Authorities including the US Coast Guard responded to the crash at approximately 11.30am on Wednesday. According to the USCG, the helicopter – a Robinson R44 II – was carrying three people and crashed in the waters of Biscayne Bay, east of Miami executive airport.
“1 person is reported deceased & 2 people were transported by EMS to a higher level of care,” the USCG said .

The Miami-Dade sheriff’s office also confirmed the crash, saying : “@MiamiDadeFire, @CityofMiamiFire, and Key Biscayne Fire Rescue responded to the scene as part of a coordinated emergency response. Three individuals were involved in the incident, and emergency personnel worked together to provide assistance.”

According to Miami-Dade fire rescue, two adult patients with traumatic injuries were transported by ground rescue units from Miami fire rescue and Key Biscayne fire rescue to a designated landing zone, where MDFR air rescue flew them to the main trauma center.
Aerial footage shared online showed the helicopter submerged upside down in the water, with its yellow emergency floats still attached.
The National Transportation Safety Board said that it was investigating the crash.
The Guardian has approached the Federal Aviation Administration for additional comment.

The crash came just days after a business jet carrying nine people crashed in Greenacres, in Florida’s Palm Beach county, on Sunday, killing everyone on board. Shortly before the crash, the crew reported accumulating ice, turbulence and precipitation before declaring a mayday. As the aircraft rapidly lost altitude, the pilot warned air traffic control that the jet was in an overspeed condition before nose-diving into the ground.

title_en: Biden’s revenge: His alumni are winning in the midterms
title_zh: Biden’s revenge: His alumni are winning in the midterms
summary: The former president wasn’t a prominent force on the trail, but some of his one-time staffers have won high profile races on Tuesday night.
summary_zh: The former president wasn’t a prominent force on the trail, but some of his one-time staffers have won high profile races on Tuesday night.
body_en: Joe Biden was unceremoniously ushered out of the White House two years ago.
On Tuesday, he got a small measure of revenge.

Prominent Biden administration alumni are winning in a handful of notable races, with Keisha Lance Bottoms — the one-time Atlanta mayor turned Biden’s senior adviser and director of the Office of Public Engagement — leading the pack by flipping Georgia’s governorship.
The victories, his former staffers say, are an important part of rehabilitating his legacy within a Democratic Party that all but banished him in 2024.

“It's proof that President Biden assembled a talented team of public servants — who the public is calling on now to help turn this country around,” said Ron Klain, Biden’s former chief of staff. “These fantastic men and women will make life more affordable, health care more available, protect our rights, fight corruption, and make our country stronger.”

Biden was not a regular on the trail this year, and most Democrats kept their distance from the former president. But he did weigh in on a handful of primaries, helping put loyal lieutenants in front of voters who still held him in high regard.

While Bottoms was the highest profile victory, there’s a number of Biden alumni also poised to head to Washington. Gabe Amo, who won a 2023 special election in a blue Rhode Island seat, secured his second full term in Congress. And Dan Koh, who won Massachusetts’ 6th District to succeed Rep. Seth Moulton, was Biden’s deputy Cabinet secretary and deputy director of the White House Office of Intergovernmental Affairs.
He leaned into his Biden endorsement throughout the campaign and this week reposted a video of a phone call he and his family had with Joe and Jill Biden on primary night in September.

“Mr. President and Madame first lady, thank you so much for all of your support,” he told them. “It wouldn’t have been possible without both of you. … You changed my life by giving me a job of a lifetime. And you got my back the minute I decided to run.”

Biden’s Cabinet also had a strong night in other governor races. Xavier Becerra, Biden’s secretary of Health and Human Services, had a solid polling lead over Republican Steve Hilton in the race to be California’s next governor going into Tuesday. And, Deb Haaland, Biden’s Interior secretary, was projected to win the New Mexico governor race.

"In his farewell speech, President Biden warned that ‘an oligarchy is taking shape in America of extreme wealth, power, and influence that literally threatens our entire democracy,’” said Andrew Bates, the former president’s longtime spokesperson. “He urged his team and supporters to keep standing up for the values that we all care about, including decency, hard work, and a sense of national community. On the ballot and off, a whole lot of his alumni are fighting to carry on that legacy.”
