Mike Johnson will step aside as top House Republican After Tuesday's bruising defeat for Republicans, House Speaker Mike Johnson will not stay on as minority leader come January.
Mike Johnson will step aside as top House Republican next Congress
House Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., speaks with reporters alongside President Trump on Nov. 1, 2026, at Dubuque Regional Airport in Dubuque, Iowa. Jacquelyn Martin/AP hide caption
Midterms coverage: Live results | Takeaways | Stories around the country

After a bruising defeat for Republicans, House Speaker Mike Johnson does not plan to stay on as Republican leader in the new Congress, according to a source familiar with his plans who was not authorized to discuss them publicly.
The Louisiana Republican served two terms as speaker, elected after his predecessor, California Rep. Kevin McCarthy, was ousted in 2023 .
Johnson's decision will open a role for the top House leadership position in the minority. Republicans are scheduled to hold their leadership elections on Nov. 10.

Historically, the president's party loses seats in midterm elections. The blue wave soared past the expectations of many in Washington, flipping seats in traditionally red states that the president has won previously.
Johnson nodded to that history in remarks Tuesday night.

"From the first day of this election, we knew that to keep the House and sustain our majority, we would have to defy more than a century of midterm history. It's only happened twice in 90 years that a sitting president has picked up or held seats for his party in that first two-year cycle. There's a lot of reasons for it. It's very, very difficult to overcome, and it looks like history will be kept tonight," he said.

Johnson worked closely with the Trump administration throughout his tenure as speaker, and endured the balancing act of trying to keep his conference united with the narrowest of majorities. His razor thin majority meant even one Republican defection meant GOP priorities were at risk.

That dynamic will not be replicated for the presumptive next House Speaker, Rep. Hakeem Jeffries of New York. While there are a handful of lawmakers elected with support of the Democratic Socialists of America , eager to push the party further to the left, the comfortable margin for Jeffries means he will likely be able to achieve his priorities, even with defections.
His speakership would be history making — he would be the first Black lawmaker elected to the position .

title_en: Tuesday’s elections bring historic first for Black governors
title_zh: Tuesday’s elections bring historic first for Black governors
summary: Wins by Byron Donalds in Florida, Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia and Wes Moore in Maryland mean multiple Black governors will serve simultaneously for the first time.
summary_zh: Wins by Byron Donalds in Florida, Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia and Wes Moore in Maryland mean multiple Black governors will serve simultaneously for the first time.
body_en: Tuesday’s elections bring historic first for Black governors
Nov. 3, 2026, 9:15 PM EST / Updated Nov. 4, 2026, 5:49 AM EST
For the first time in U.S. history, multiple elected Black governors will serve at the same time after five wins in elections across the country.

They are Democrat Wes Moore, who won re-election in Maryland, Republican Rep. Byron Donalds in Florida, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia, Democrat David Crowley in Wisconsin and Democrat Aaron Ford in Nevada.

Before those wins, the only elected Black governors in U.S. history had been Moore; Deval Patrick, a Democrat who was elected Massachusetts’ governor in 2006; and Doug Wilder, a Democrat who was elected Virginia’s governor in 1989. None served simultaneously.

Bottoms, the former mayor of Atlanta, overcame an enormous spending disadvantage to defeat Republican Rick Jackson, a wealthy healthcare executive who pumped more than $100 million of his own money into his campaign. She is the first woman and the first Black person to be elected governor of Georgia, and will be the first Black female governor in U.S. history.
Full speech: Keisha Lance Bottoms projected winner in Georgia governor's race
In an interview with NBC News last month , Donalds said the history-making aspect of his candidacy was “very special.”

“From a larger perspective, there’s so much that has been talked about in politics over the last couple decades around race. Obviously, the country has had some real negative parts of our history surrounding race,” he said. “I’m humbled to be in this position, but I think it says a lot more about the state [of Florida] than it does about me.”
In South Carolina, another Black Democrat, state Rep. Jermaine Johnson, lost his state’s race for governor to Republican Alan Wilson.

On the Republican side, Rep. John James lost his governor’s race to Democrat Jocelyn Benson, and Minnesota state House Speaker Lisa Demuth lost the state’s gubernatorial contest to Democrat Amy Klobuchar.

Given what state lawmakers have focused on in recent years, my coverage areas tend to veer into reproductive rights, voting rights and education policy. I was born and raised in Milwaukee, and I try to make my native state proud by covering as many of its fascinating political stories as I can.

title_zh: Back in the majority, Democrats have plans for a long list of Trump investigations
summary: Democrats will have the ability to subpoena records and compel individuals to testify. The Epstein files, Elon Musk, the Iran war and Trump's business interests may all come under the microscope.
summary_zh: Democrats will have the ability to subpoena records and compel individuals to testify. The Epstein files, Elon Musk, the Iran war and Trump's business interests may all come under the microscope.
body_en: Back in the majority, Democrats have plans for a long list of Trump investigations

President Trump speaks at a midterm campaign rally in Daytona Beach, Fla. on October 30, 2026. Democrats are planning a long list of investigations against the president in the new Congress. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Midterms coverage: Live results | Takeaways | Stories around the country
Democrats won big in the midterm elections, but with President Trump still in the White House, the next Congress is unlikely to see much major legislation signed into law.

Instead, expect to see a lot more oversight. With public corruption and failing leadership as two of the top issues concerning voters, congressional Democrats have an ambitious agenda of investigations planned for their return to power in the House and Senate.

Their new majorities mean that they will have at their disposal the full investigatory powers of the Congress, which include the ability to subpoena records for review and compel individuals to testify before lawmakers.
Democrats win full control of Congress, ushering in a new era of divided government
Rep. Robert Garcia, the California Democrat who is expected to become chair of the House Oversight committee, put it bluntly in a statement: "LAWYER UP."

The Democratic Party has a long list of investigative targets. According to conversations with Democratic House and Senate committee staffers, here are some areas the party is likely to prioritize in its oversight work.

Among Democrats' primary targets: the administration's handling of — and connections to — the scandals of late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Bipartisan congressional action forced the Trump administration to release extensive documents tied to federal investigations of Epstein's crimes and other alleged offenses, though Democrats maintain that many of the records were improperly redacted or withheld from the public. They also say that the Justice Department has worked to shield Trump from damaging allegations — claims that the department's leadership has denied.

In the new Congress, lawmakers are expected to probe ties between Epstein and other powerful figures, including the president himself, which they say is part of an effort to secure accountability for victims of Epstein's crimes.

In connection with an October report , Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee, said, "Donald Trump says he knew Jeffrey Epstein 'just like everybody in Palm Beach knew him.' Not exactly."
"Evidence involving 11 women tells a completely different and far more damning story about their relationship and the abuse of young women and girls that took place in their network," Raskin said.

The president, for his part, has long denied any wrongdoing related to Epstein and has maintained that their relationship ended before the disgraced financier was indicted for soliciting prostitution in 2016.

Democrats also plan to continue their own investigations into what they describe as efforts by administration officials to advance the financial interests of the president, his family, themselves and close allies.

In particular, Democrats highlight the president's continued business interests, including Truth Social, a number of cryptocurrency projects and overseas projects involving his sons and powerful foreign investors.

Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., speaks to the press on Capitol Hill on June 10, 2026. Garcia is expected to become chair of the House Oversight Committee in the new Congress. Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images hide caption

Garcia on the House Oversight Committee, has gone further, linking the high cost of living to politicians on both sides of the aisle acting in their own self-interest rather than the interest of the American public.

"Millions of dollars in dark money are flowing throughout our political system. Some members of Congress may be trading stocks based on information the public doesn't have. The revolving door between the government and lobbying for large corporations keeps spinning," he wrote last month in an MS Now opinion piece . "Americans are dealing with a cost-of-living crisis, and these abuses of power are making it worse. All the while, the wealthiest people in our country are richer than ever."

Trump returned to office promising a stricter approach to immigration in the United States. But public support for his deportation agenda has cratered in the wake of a number of high-profile incidents involving federal immigration enforcement personnel, including the killing of two U.S. citizens in Minnesota this year.

summary: Democrats won secretary of state contests in four presidential battlegrounds while making inroads in red territory, giving them election oversight authority in key states for the 2028 elections.

body_en: Democrats score key secretary of state wins ahead of the 2028 election
Democrats won secretary of state contests in four presidential battlegrounds while making inroads in red territory, giving them election oversight authority in key states for the 2028 elections.

Democratic candidates maintained control of secretary of state offices in Arizona, Michigan and Nevada, while flipping the office in Georgia, all states that have been at the center of recent campaigns for the White House. And Democrats gained secretary of state control in the GOP-leaning states of Indiana and Ohio.

In Georgia, Democrat Penny Brown Reynolds will succeed Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger, who drew President Donald Trump’s ire for rebuffing his push to overturn the state’s 2020 election results. She defeated state Rep. Tim Fleming, a former aide to outgoing Republican Gov. Brian Kemp who was endorsed by Trump.

Reynolds, who is known for a family court television show and serving in the Biden administration, campaigned as a judge who would stand up to Trump while following the law in running state elections. Fleming did not go as far as other Republicans in claiming the 2020 election was stolen, but said there were “irregularities” and called for new mail voting restrictions.

In Michigan, Democratic Lt. Gov Garlin Gilchrist bested Macomb County Clerk Anthony Forlini, a Republican, to succeed Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson, who won the state’s race for governor. Gilchrist had criticized Forlini for sharing voter data with the Trump administration and hiring a Jan. 6 protester to his office.

In Arizona and Nevada, incumbent Democrats Adrian Fontes and Cisco Aguilar fended off challenges from far-right Republicans whose careers were rooted in advancing election conspiracy theories, enjoying far better margins than they had in similar 2022 matchups.

And in Texas, Democrat Gina Hinojosa’s win in the governor’s race is also expected to give the party authority over the administration of state elections. Texas’ secretary of state is appointed by the governor, with concurrent terms.

Once an under-the-radar, downballot job, secretary of state has become a much more high-profile position amid a constant drumbeat of unfounded election fraud claims from Trump and his allies. All four battleground states saw challenges to the 2020 election results and secretaries of state in these and other states have faced a steady stream of lawsuits and threats.
In the final stretch of the midterm campaign, Democrats started targeting Indiana, Kansas, Ohio and Iowa for red-state gains. So far, they’ve won two of their targets and lost one.

Democratic state Rep. Allison Russo will be the next secretary of state of Ohio as her party also flipped Senate and gubernatorial seats in a state that has shifted to the right in recent years. Russo defeated Republican state Treasurer Robert Sprague.

In Indiana, Beau Bayh, a 30-year-old scion of a longtime Democratic family in the state, beat Republican state Rep. Max Engling. Engling had replaced Indiana’s Republican incumbent, Diego Morales, who was embroiled in allegations of corruption and ethics violations, at the party’s nominating convention.

Bayh spent more than $ 8.6 million on ads, according to AdImpact, campaigning heavily on fighting corruption. He ran at the top of the ticket in Indiana, which didn’t have any races for Senate or governor this year.

In Kansas, where voters haven’t elected a Democrat as secretary of state since 1948, the race between Democratic state Rep. Jennifer Day and Republican state Rep. Pat Proctor was too close to call, according to NBC News’ Decision Desk.
Democrats saw success elsewhere in the state, with pastor Adam Hamilton pulling off an upset over GOP Sen. Roger Marshall.
Top-of-the-ticket wins didn’t translate to secretary of state success everywhere.
In Iowa, Republican Secretary of State Paul Pate fended off a challenge from Democrat Ryan Peterman, even as Democrats won Senate and governor’s races in the state.
And In South Carolina, Republican Secretary of State Mark Hammond beat Democratic challenger Jason Belton, even as Democrat Annie Andrews prevailed in the Senate race.
Jane C. Timm is a senior reporter for NBC News.

Mike Johnson , the Republican speaker of the House, has said he is not planning to pursue the role of minority leader once his party loses its majority in the chamber, according to multiple reports.

What can Democrats actually do now they have won Congress?

Reports of his decision to rule out a bid for minority leader emerged after Fox News reported that the Ohio Republican Jim Jordan, chair of the House judiciary committee, was planning an effort to oust Johnson to take the position of minority leader, citing two people familiar with the matter.

It would not be the first time that Jordan has gunned for the House Republicans’ top job. Jordan previously sought to claim the title after Kevin McCarthy, the previous Republican speaker of the House, lost the job in 2023, but failed to net enough votes from members of the chamber.

Multiple outlets, including Punchbowl News and Fox News, reported that the Louisiana representative Steve Scalise, Republicans’ majority leader, was a candidate for the minority leader job. Like Jordan, Scalise vied for the speaker of the House position after it was vacated by Kevin McCarthy in 2023.

Billionaire Leon Black has filed a federal defamation lawsuit against California Rep. Robert Garcia for public comments the Democratic congressman made tying him to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein

NEW YORK -- Billionaire Leon Black on Wednesday filed a federal defamation lawsuit against California Rep. Robert Garcia for public comments the Democratic congressman made tying him to disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein .

The court filing comes less than two months after the House approved a resolution holding Black in contempt of Congress for defying the Oversight Committee’s subpoenas in its investigation into Epstein.
In June, Black appeared for a voluntary interview at the committee during which he denied any knowledge of Epstein's sex trafficking network.

Weeks later, Garcia said during a TV interview that “Leon Black is at the center of Jeffrey Epstein’s crimes” and that Black “was one of the last people to actually interact" with Epstein before he committed suicide in prison.
In addition, Garcia said that he had “talked to survivors that have credibly named Leon Black as someone that was involved in direct abuse of women and was directly involved" with Epstein.

Those statements were false and were made maliciously, Black asserts through his lawyers. The defamation lawsuit filed in U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York seeks a jury trial and $7.25 million in compensatory and punitive damages.

“Congressman Garcia’s knowing lies have caused real and significant ongoing harm to Mr. Black. His physical safety has been threatened, he has received a barrage of hateful calls, emails, and social media posts, and his business and philanthropic endeavors have suffered,” the filing states.
Garcia’s office didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment on the lawsuit.
In September, Garcia called the contempt resolution against Black “an important step toward justice and accountability.”

The election led to several historic firsts. In New Hampshire, Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man to be elected to the Senate. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms will be the first Black woman governor. And in New Mexico, Deb Haaland will make history as the first Native American woman to serve as a governor. As have been reporting, yesterday's election brought a number of historic firsts. In New Hampshire, Chris Pappas became the first openly gay man elected to the U.S. Senate. In Colorado, Melat Kiros became the first Generation Z woman elected to Congress. And, in Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor.

Among those making history is Deb Haaland, who will become the first Native American woman to serve as governor of any U.S. state. Haaland previously served as interior secretary under President Biden and was one of the first Native American women elected to Congress.
Congratulations on your victory and welcome back to the "News Hour."

You made history, of course, but voters are also expecting results. So how will you balance the symbolism of this victory with the responsibility now of governing a state that has faced persistent challenges? So many people are dealing with the high cost of living, persistent challenges with poverty, education, access to health care.
How are you planning to deliver tangible results in New Mexico?
Absolutely. Thank you so much for the question and for having me.

And, of course, very proud to be the first Native American woman governor in the history of our country. That wasn't why I was running, though, of course. I have so much experience, having served at the highest level of government as the secretary of the interior, where I managed a work force of 70,000, an $18 billion annual budget.

And, yes, like the rest of the country, our state is facing steep Medicaid cuts; 89,000 people can be kicked off the Medicaid rolls come the beginning of the year, people losing their SNAP benefits. This is all the result of the Trump bill that passed earlier this year.

And so, of course, we want to make sure that we're stepping up, the legislature and myself continuing to fill in the gaps that our governor now has worked to fill in. We know that prices are getting higher due to so many of the tariffs and the war in Iran making gas prices higher. New Mexicans are paying higher costs for everything.

And so we want to put more money in the pockets of New Mexicans, enhancing the child tax credit, the working families tax credit, continuing to move our clean energy forward, which we know will lower utility costs. So there's a lot of work to do, but I'm confident that we can get there.

Democrats had a strong election night across the country. How much of your victory, in your view, was a rejection of President Trump and his approach, and how much of it was an endorsement of your own vision for New Mexico?

Well, we currently have a Democratic governor here in New Mexico. Generally, every eight years -- our governor is termed out the end of this year. Every eight years, the seat flips back to Republican.

And New Mexicans realized that yes, we needed to keep going on the trajectory that we are going on. We have universal childcare. We have early childhood education for every child in New Mexico. And those are things that New Mexicans feel have made their lives better.

And so I want to ensure that we can enhance those programs, expand them across the state, so that every New Mexico family has an opportunity to participate. Universal childcare, it's an economic driver all over New Mexico. It creates jobs and helps parents to know their kids are safe while they're at work.
So it's a win-win for our state and the people of New Mexico, and we will continue down that path.

I wonder, what have you learned from your time in Washington, both in Congress and in the Cabinet, about what government gets right and what it gets wrong, and how does all of that shape your approach to governing?

title_en: ‘We forgot what it's like to be populist’: Republicans see Trump’s 2024 crumbling
title_zh: “我们忘记了民粹主义是什么感觉”：共和党人认为特朗普的2024年计划正在崩溃
summary: New results from the POLITICO Poll show that one in 10 Trump voters are planning to vote for Democrats on Tuesday.
summary_zh: 政治民意调查的新结果显示，十分之一的特朗普选民计划在周二投票给民主党。
body_en: Republicans’ 2024 coalition is cracking in real time.

President Donald Trump roared back into office two years ago after making major gains with young voters and Americans of color. Now those key groups appear to be moving away from him amid an unpopular Iran war and his lagging approval ratings, according to new results from the POLITICO Poll conducted by PF Global.
Roughly 9% of Trump 2024 voters plan to cast their ballot for a Democrat this year, compared with just over 2% of former Vice President Kamala Harris’ voters who now plan to back Republicans.
Underlying that shift is a lack of enthusiasm from two groups central to Trump’s win: Latinos and young people.

At the end of last year, 56% of Hispanic Trump voters identified as MAGA Republicans. As of this October, just 37% still do, revealing a frustration with the label that denotes some of the president’s most loyal supporters.
At the end of last year, 50% of young Trump voters ages 20 to 29 said they were certain to vote. As of this October, just 38% say this.
It’s an alarming sign for the party heading into election night, as Republicans race to save deep-red seats across the map and juice turnout among the MAGA base to avoid unthinkable losses.

The scramble on the campaign trail reveals the extent of the concern. Speaker Mike Johnson is making one final campaign swing through South Texas on Tuesday, where Republicans have been racing to assuage Hispanic voters’ concerns over mass deportations and the economy. GOP officials are fretting about the impact of lingering inflation and high prices on working-class voters of all races, including young men they’re scared to death won’t show up to the polls in strong enough numbers.

They’re also pouring millions of last-minute dollars into a series of southern states with large Black populations whose voters appear to be surging to the polls in record numbers — like Mississippi, South Carolina and even Louisiana — to shore them up.
“The coalition that we built under Trump doesn't fucking exist anymore,” said Gina Swoboda, a longtime Trump ally and former chair of the Arizona Republican Party.

The White House has been trying to stem the bleeding within the Trump coalition of voters: The president has barnstormed a series of largely red states and is holding a flurry of tele-rallies in the final days.

“Two years ago, Trump and other Republicans had a play with those voters because they were frustrated with Biden and Harris; two years later, things might be less bad than they were two years ago — but they're still concerned,” said Scott Walker, the Republican former governor of Wisconsin and 2016 presidential candidate who now leads the conservative Young America's Foundation.
White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said Trump has “crisscrossed the country” campaigning for Republicans and drawing a contrast with “the radical-left Democrats.”
“President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party,” Bis added.

Natalie Baldassarre, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, said in a statement that the “Trump administration has delivered on its promises to the American people” and the president “has barnstormed the nation to tout these achievements.”
GOP Latino voters start to shed the ‘MAGA’ label

The durability of Republicans’ 2024 coalition is a crucial test for the party’s future. Republicans’ inroads with young, Latino and Black voters propelled the party into a trifecta of power in Washington, and keeping those gains will be key to the GOP’s bid to hold onto power. A regression in support from those groups could send Republicans back to the drawing board as they craft a winning formula for the 2028 presidential election.
Top Republicans are incredibly worried about losing their grip on Hispanic voters, as they try to stave off a bloodbath in South Texas, losses across key Florida House seats and more.

There’s been a 19-point drop between last November and this October of Hispanic Trump voters who identify as MAGA, part of Trump’s core base, according to the poll. While two-thirds of these voters still intend to vote for Republicans in the midterm election, their dissatisfaction with Trump’s agenda is clear.

The survey found that Hispanic Trump voters are more likely than non-Hispanic Trump voters to have voted for Democrats in the past decade — and think the Trump administration’s mass deportations are too aggressive.
body_zh: 共和党的2024年联盟正在实时破裂。
两年前，唐纳德·特朗普(Donald Trump)总统在与年轻选民和有色人种美国人取得重大进展后，咆哮着重新上任。根据PF Global进行的政治民意调查的新结果，在不受欢迎的伊朗战争和他的支持率落后的情况下，这些关键群体似乎正在远离他。
大约9%的特朗普2024选民计划今年投票给民主党人，而前副总统卡马拉·哈里斯的选民中只有略高于2%的人现在计划支持共和党人。
这种转变的背后是对特朗普获胜至关重要的两个群体缺乏热情：拉丁裔和年轻人。
去年年底，56% 的西班牙裔特朗普选民认为自己是“MAGA”共和党人。截至今年 10 月，只有 37% 的人仍然这样做，这表明他们对总统一些最忠实支持者的标签感到失望。
去年年底，20岁至29岁的年轻特朗普选民中有50%表示他们肯定会投票。截至今年 10 月，只有 38% 的人这么说。
对于进入选举之夜的共和党来说，这是一个令人震惊的迹象，因为共和党人竞相挽救地图上的深红色席位，并提高“让美国再次伟大”基地的投票率，以避免难以想象的损失。
竞选过程中的争夺揭示了人们担忧的程度。众议院议长迈克·约翰逊将于周二在德克萨斯州南部进行最后一次竞选活动，共和党人一直在竞相缓解拉美裔选民对大规模驱逐出境和经济的担忧。共和党官员担心持续的通货膨胀和高物价对各族工薪阶层选民的影响，其中包括年轻人，他们担心不会有足够多的人参加投票。
他们还在最后一刻向一系列拥有大量黑人人口的南部各州投入了数百万美元，这些州的投票站投票人数似乎创下了历史新高——比如密西西比州、南卡罗来纳州，甚至路易斯安那州——以支持他们。
“我们在特朗普领导下建立的联盟已经不复存在了，”特朗普的长期盟友、亚利桑那州共和党前主席吉娜·斯沃博达说。
白宫一直在努力阻止特朗普选民联盟内部的流血：总统对一系列主要是红色的州进行了巡回演讲，并在最后几天举行了一系列电话集会。
“两年前，特朗普和其他共和党人对这些选民进行了玩弄，因为他们对拜登和哈里斯感到沮丧；两年后，情况可能没有两年前那么糟糕，但他们仍然感到担忧，”共和党前威斯康星州州长、2016 年总统候选人斯科特·沃克 (Scott Walker) 表示，他现在是保守派青年美国基金会的负责人。
白宫发言人劳伦·比斯表示，特朗普“走遍全国”为共和党竞选，并与“激进左翼民主党”形成鲜明对比。
“特朗普总统是共和党明确的领导人、最好的使者和无与伦比的动力，”比斯补充道。
共和党全国委员会发言人娜塔莉·巴尔达萨尔在一份声明中表示，“特朗普政府已经兑现了对美国人民的承诺”，总统“已经在全国范围内宣传这些成就”。
共和党拉丁裔选民开始摆脱“MAGA”标签
共和党2024年联盟的持久性是对该党未来的关键考验。共和党在年轻、拉丁裔和黑人选民中的影响力推动该党在华盛顿获得了三重权力，而保持这些成果将是共和党保住权力的关键。如果这些团体的支持率下降，共和党人可能会重新从头开始制定 2028 年总统选举的制胜方案。
共和党高层非常担心失去对拉美裔选民的控制，因为他们试图避免德克萨斯州南部发生大屠杀、佛罗里达州众议院关键席位的流失等。
民意调查显示，从去年 11 月到今年 10 月，支持特朗普核心基础的西班牙裔特朗普选民数量下降了 19 个百分点。尽管其中三分之二的选民仍打算在中期选举中投票给共和党，但他们对特朗普议程的不满是显而易见的。
调查发现，拉美裔特朗普选民比非拉美裔特朗普选民在过去十年中更有可能投票给民主党，并认为特朗普政府的大规模驱逐出境过于激进。

title_en: AI PACs spent millions trying to shape Congress — here’s how they fared
title_zh: AI PACs spent millions trying to shape Congress — here’s how they fared
summary: AI industry PACs spent millions influencing the 2026 midterms, with mixed results. Political groups are already looking toward the next election cycle.
summary_zh: AI industry PACs spent millions influencing the 2026 midterms, with mixed results. Political groups are already looking toward the next election cycle.
body_en: Political groups both supporting and opposing the AI industry spent millions of dollars trying to influence Tuesday’s midterm elections and shape the future of AI regulation. That spending produced mixed results, with some of the most heavily backed candidates losing their races.

On the industry side, two AI-focused political action committees (PACs) that raised and spent money to influence the elections — American Mission and Building the Future — collectively spent $4.8 million to back South Carolina Senate candidate Darline Graham, who lost. American Mission is the Republican spending arm of Leading the Future (LTF), a broader political group backed by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and the VC firm Andreessen Horowitz.

American Mission also spent more than $500,000 apiece supporting Republican House candidates Aaron Flint in Montana and Laurie Buckhout in North Carolina, both of whom lost. LTF’s Democratic spending arm, Think Big, had better luck backing Florida Rep. Jared Moskowitz, who won reelection.

Groups advocating for stronger AI safeguards also saw mixed results. Public First, which is backed by Anthropic, supported several Republicans who lost through its affiliated PAC but had more success backing Democratic candidates. It also contributed $3 million to a PAC supporting California state Sen. Scott Wiener, who was leading his race at the time of publication.

Meanwhile, Guardrails Alliance , a group that has sought to make taking money from AI companies a political liability, spent more than $1 million apiece opposing two candidates who lost: California Rep. Jimmy Gomez and Montana’s Aaron Flint. It also spent $300,000 supporting Angela Gonzales-Torres, who defeated Gomez.

It’s difficult to separate the impact of AI-related spending from the broader Democratic wave that swept Tuesday’s elections. Elon Musk, who reportedly poured half a billion dollars into supporting Republicans in the midterms, also saw many of his candidates lose . Indeed, LTF also backed some candidates it believed were likely to win, only to see them lose to the Dems.

For LTF, though, the general election wasn’t the main focus. The group told TechCrunch ahead of Election Day that it thinks primaries (the contests that choose each party’s nominee) are a more effective use of its money, because spending there can build name recognition and help candidates set up AI policy agendas.

LTF spent $27.38 million in the primaries, including $8 million alone on opposing New York Assembly member Alex Bores , who lost his bid for Congress back in June. When deciding whether it’s worth jumping into a general election race, LTF assesses how competitive the race is, whether it thinks spending could make a difference, and whether it should keep its powder dry for future elections.
Charlie Blaettler, political director of Guardrails Alliance, had a different theory for why LTF spent comparatively little in the general election.

“They don’t want their money to become an issue in these elections,” he said. He pointed to the Michigan Senate primary election, in which a pro-Israel lobbying group called AIPAC spent close to $30 million backing Democratic candidate Haley Stevens against Abdul El-Sayed. Stevens conceded the primary to El-Sayed, who went on to win the Senate seat.

“AIPAC became the story in that race,” Blaettler said. “We know people hate AI billionaires. They hate the people running these companies. They’re very distrustful and disgusted by the political spending and lobbying that the tech industry does. If they spend in a competitive race, they would just become an enormous liability for their candidates.”

The main fight among AIPACs, whether they are pro-industry or pro-regulation, is whether Congress should establish a national AI framework that overrides state laws , or whether states will maintain their own ability to impose safeguards.

Neither side seems poised to back down. LTF, which favors a single national AI framework, told TechCrunch it plans to keep spending in the 2028 elections, while Guardrails Alliance says it wants to keep opposing candidates backed by the AI industry.

Blaettler said that while LTF’s ads rarely touch on AI, instead focusing on popular issues for each candidate, Guardrail Alliance’s ads are specifically about who is taking money from the AI industry.
“Our goal is to make AI money politically toxic,” Blaettler said.

title_zh: Big Tech claims voters’ AI backlash is “anti-Trump” not “anti-tech”
summary: Tech industry in denial as US overwhelmingly votes to restrict AI, data centers.
summary_zh: Tech industry in denial as US overwhelmingly votes to restrict AI, data centers.
body_en: Donald Trump’s big, rapid American AI buildout now faces a major slowdown as voters in yesterday’s elections overwhelmingly supported candidates and measures that favored increasing restrictions on AI and data centers nationwide.

One resource from a polling firm, called Redbud Consulting, tracked data center initiatives on the ballot and reported that out of 44 measures across 10 states seeking to restrict data centers, 38 passed so far. Those measures included dozens of moratoriums and bans. Analysts suggested those won’t impact data centers already under construction or approved through 2027, instead largely impacting future projects planned for 2028. Only one measure passed allowing a data center to proceed. But even that small win represented pushback on the AI industry—requiring data center developers in a North Dakota city to pay for independent reviews and hold public hearings when expanding or proposing projects.
In addition to increasing regulations on data centers, voters also backed anti-AI candidates, electing officials vowing crackdowns in key states building out the most data center capacity in the US.
